titre: The Hidden Debt of the Gift
accroche: A gift that is never returned eventually costs the relationship itself.
contenu_vulgarise:
Someone gives you an unexpected gift. You thank them, sincerely. And yet something in you is already taking note: you will have to return the favor. Not right away, not necessarily in kind, but one day. This discreet, almost universal discomfort is the starting point of one of the founding texts of anthropology: Marcel Mauss's *Essai sur le don* (*The Gift*), published in 1925 in *L'Année Sociologique*.

## Three Obligations, Not Generosity

Mauss compares ethnographies from Polynesia, Melanesia, and the American Northwest Coast, and draws from them a common mechanism that he sums up as three linked obligations: to give, to receive, to return. Giving commits one to a relationship. Receiving accepts it. Refusing a gift, in most of the societies he studies, amounts to refusing the bond itself, almost a declaration of hostility. Returning, finally, closes the cycle, but rarely in kind: the return gift is often slightly greater, which restarts the exchange rather than ending it.

The case that struck Mauss most comes from New Zealand. A Maori sage, Tamati Ranaipiri, explains to the ethnographer Elsdon Best why a given object (a *taonga*) must eventually return to its first owner: it carries within it the *hau*, something of the giver's spirit, which “wants” to go back home. The vocabulary is religious; the use Mauss makes of it is sociological. The hau is not a magical force one would have to believe is real. It is the way a society without written contracts gives itself a reason to return.

## What This Shifts

The point of the demonstration is theoretical: Mauss aims directly at the idea of a pure, disinterested gift with nothing in return. This is the very idea that the classical economics of his day attributed, in inverted mirror image, to market exchange. There is no such thing, he shows, as a gift that does not create a debt. This debt is not a flaw of the gift. It is what makes it a social bond rather than a mere transfer of an object.

Its echo can be found wherever a gift embarrasses more than it delights: the business gift one hesitates to accept because it obligates, international aid never quite without conditions, the invitation one cannot decline without losing something of the relationship. The word “free” hides, most of the time, an account that remains open. And it is precisely this open account that holds the social bond together, whereas a settled payment obligates no one to anything. Mauss was writing against an idea of his time; the idea he fought has not disappeared.

repere.texte: Published in 1925 in L'Année Sociologique, the essay draws on ethnographies of Polynesia, Melanesia, and the American Northwest Coast to establish the threefold obligation of giving, receiving, and returning.
repere.source: Marcel Mauss, Essai sur le don. Forme et raison de l'échange dans les sociétés archaïques (The Gift: The Form and Reason for Exchange in Archaic Societies), 1925

carte.idee: As early as 1925, Marcel Mauss showed that a gift always creates a debt: you must receive it on pain of offense, and return it on pain of rupture. The word “free” almost always hides an account left open.

quiz.question: According to Mauss, what does one risk by refusing a gift in the societies he studies?
choix: The gift is simply canceled with no other consequence
The refusal amounts to implicit acceptance of a deferred return gift
The refusal amounts to a declaration of hostility toward the giver
The giver must then return the object to his own group
quiz.explication: Mauss shows that receiving is an obligation just like giving: refusing a gift amounts, in the societies he studies, to refusing the relationship itself, which can be perceived as a rupture, even an open declaration of hostility.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the hau designate, in the explanation given by Tamati Ranaipiri?
choix: The price at which a taonga is exchanged for another good
Something of the giver's spirit, which wants to go back home
The name of the return gift that the recipient must prepare
The ceremony during which a gift is handed over
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Maori sage explains to the ethnographer Elsdon Best that a given object, the taonga, carries within it the hau, something of the giver's spirit, which wants to return to its starting point. This is what obliges one, sooner or later, to give back.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What use does Mauss make of this religious notion?
choix: He sees in it proof that a belief acts physically on objects
He rejects it as a late invention of the early ethnographers
He reads in it how a society without written contracts gives itself a reason to return
He reserves it for the Maori case alone, with no reach beyond New Zealand
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The vocabulary is religious; the use Mauss makes of it is sociological. He does not ask us to believe in a magical force: he shows how a society that does not write its contracts gives itself a reason to return.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does the return gift not truly close the exchange?
choix: Because it is often a little greater, which restarts the cycle
Because it must be returned the same day, or it does not count
Because it is never accepted by the original giver
Because it must be strictly identical to the gift received
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Returning closes the cycle, but rarely in kind: the return gift is often slightly greater than what was received, so that the debt changes sides instead of being extinguished, and the exchange starts up again.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Against what idea of his time does Mauss write?
choix: Against the idea that the gift creates a lasting social bond
Against the practice of comparing societies very distant from one another
Against the thesis of a return gift greater than the gift received
Against the idea of a pure, disinterested gift with nothing in return
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Mauss aims at the idea of a free gift, which the economics of his time set in inverted mirror image against market exchange. He shows that no gift comes without a debt, and that it is precisely this debt that makes it a social bond rather than a mere transfer of an object.
